hook: The alternating harmonic series $1 - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} - \cdots$ converges, but strip the signs and you get the harmonic series, which diverges. Some series converge because their terms are small; others converge only because their signs keep cancelling. Telling the two apart is what absolute and conditional convergence are about.

options: Yes, by the alternating series test
No, by the nth term test
prereq.why: The sizes $\frac{1}{n}$ decrease and approach 0, and the signs alternate.

figure.caption: Same sizes, different signs: $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ climbs without bound, while $\sum \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ settles near $0.693$.

chain.cause: Take the absolute value of every term
chain.effect: $\sum |a_n|$ is a series of positive terms, which the comparison, integral and ratio tests can decide
$\sum a_n$ converges too (absolutely): signs can only cancel, never add
the convergence comes from the signs cancelling: conditional convergence
its terms can be rearranged in any order without changing the sum

ideas: Absolutely convergent: $\sum |a_n|$ converges. Conditionally convergent: $\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum |a_n|$ diverges.
To classify: test $\sum |a_n|$ first. If it converges, you are done (absolute). If not, test $\sum a_n$ itself, usually with the alternating series test.
A divergent $\sum |a_n|$ alone decides nothing about $\sum a_n$.

misconception.right: A divergent series of absolute values only rules out absolute convergence. The signed series converges by the alternating series test, so it converges conditionally.

summary: Every series is absolutely convergent ($\sum |a_n|$ converges), conditionally convergent ($\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum |a_n|$ diverges), or divergent. Absolute convergence implies convergence, and an absolutely convergent series keeps its sum when its terms are rearranged.
